title: Ibn Tulun's mosque
hookLine: an old Cairo mosque with a spiral minaret

lines: A STRIP OF PAPER, ROLLED UP.
cards: Build the minaret like this. The man saying it holds up a strip of paper he's been idly rolling around his finger during a meeting, now a tight coil.
That's a story told about Ahmad ibn Tulun, who governed Egypt in the name of the Abbasid caliphs before Cairo itself existed. It may not be true.
But walk around his mosque today and the minaret does look a little like that coil: a stair wrapped around the outside of the tower, climbing as it turns.

teach.h: OLDER THAN THE CITY AROUND IT.
teach.b: Ibn Tulun built in his own capital, a settlement just south of where the Fatimids would later lay out Cairo. Over time the city grew around his mosque, so it now stands inside Cairo, older than the city around it.

teach.h: A COURTYARD OF LIGHT AND ARCHES.
teach.b: Step through the gate and the first thing is space: a huge open courtyard, plain arcades of pointed arches on every side, and a fountain in the middle for washing before prayer.
Some visitors say the plainness is the point: nothing much to look at except light, shadow and the next arch.
Then the stair. This minaret doesn't hide its steps inside. It puts them outside, so anyone looking up can see the path the caller to prayer would climb, turning and rising.

Historians link the shape to the great spiral minaret at Samarra, the Abbasid capital where, tradition says, Ibn Tulun grew up. So the paper story and the Samarra story might both explain the same thing.
A turning stair is also a good picture of remembrance, dhikr.
You go around and around, every turn almost like the last, but higher each time.

teach.h: IN THE REMEMBRANCE OF ALLAH DO HEARTS FIND REST.
teach.b: The Qur'an says it this way, in Pickthall's translation: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!"
In that picture, repeating the same words, the same prayers, the same small acts, isn't walking in a circle. It's climbing. The spiral stair.

how: The mosque of Ibn Tulun still stands in Cairo, and visitors can climb the stair on the outside of its minaret. Dhikr is practiced by repeating short phrases such as Subhan Allah.

games.q: you're Ibn Tulun, and you're asked what your minaret should look like. you're holding a strip of paper. what do you do, in the story?
o: roll the paper into a coil and hold it up.
games.why: in the story people tell, he points to the coil. it may be legend, but the stair really does wind around the outside.

practice: If there are stairs near you, climb them as slowly as you can, one step at a time; if not, sit and let your attention go round with the breath, in, out, and again.

If you pray, say a word of dhikr with each step or breath, such as Subhan Allah, glory be to God; if you don't, count them. Notice that every turn feels the same, and that you are not where you started.

wordCard.voice: Ibn Tulun. The governor of Egypt whose mosque, now inside Cairo, has a wide courtyard and a minaret whose stair winds around the outside. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: remembrance, especially the remembering of God by repeated words.

carryVoice: Your line: the spiral stair. Saying the same words again can be a way up. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!
